title: Manna (Exodus 16:1–21)
hookLine: bread from heaven each morning, enough for the day, and it rots if hoarded

cards: A month after the sea, the singing has stopped. They're in the wilderness of Sin, a stretch of desert, and the food from Egypt has run out.
The people complain to Moses and Aaron, in the King James Bible: we wish we'd died in Egypt, "when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full." Flesh pots. Pots of meat.
Slavery has become, in their memory, a buffet. Anyone who has missed a bad job because at least you knew what you were getting knows this feeling. And God's answer is not a lecture.

teach.b: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you." In the morning, when the dew lifts, the ground is covered with something small and flaky, fine as frost. The people ask each other, in Hebrew, man hu?
What is it? "It is manna: for they wist not what it was." They named their daily bread what is it.
Exodus later says it tasted like wafers made with honey. Then the rules. Gather what each person needs for one day.
Some gather more, some less, but when they measure it, "he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack." Everyone has enough.
And don't keep any till morning. Some do anyway, just in case. By morning, "it bred worms, and stank."
You can't stockpile this bread. You have to trust there'll be more tomorrow.
Christians hear this story in the Lord's Prayer: "Give us this day our daily bread." Not this year's. Today's.
Paul quotes the line about much and little when he asks one church to share with another, so that everyone has enough.
And in John's Gospel, after feeding a crowd, Jesus talks about the manna and says: "I am the bread of life." Many Christians understand communion in that light.
Not long ago, Joseph stored grain for seven years, and that was wise. Here is the other half of wisdom: some things can only be received one day at a time.

how: Christians pray "give us this day our daily bread" in the Lord's Prayer, and many read John 6, where Jesus calls himself the bread of life, alongside the manna story, especially when teaching about communion.

s: the name manna comes from a question

games.q: you're in the wilderness. the ground is covered in manna this morning. Moses says gather today's share and keep none till morning. what do you do?
o: gather extra and hide some, just in case.
gather enough for today and trust tomorrow.
gather nothing and wait for meat.
games.why: most do. some keep extra anyway, and by morning it has bred worms and stinks. this bread only comes one day at a time.

practice: Think through today, the food, the shopping, the scrolling, and find one place where you gather more than today needs, just in case. Picture taking only enough, and notice the small fear that comes with it, then notice it pass.
If you pray, you can pray the old words, give us this day our daily bread; if you don't, simply rest in enough.

wordCard.voice: Manna. From the Hebrew question man hu, what is it? The bread from heaven that came each morning in the wilderness, enough for one day.

orig.note: Hebrew: manna. Exodus links it to the question man hu, what is it?

carryVoice: Your line: enough for today. Tomorrow has its own morning, and its own bread. See you tomorrow.
